lessons.title: Warehouse Layout and Design Principles
lessons.body: A good warehouse layout saves you time and money. Start by mapping the flow of goods: receiving, storage, picking, packing, and shipping. In Africa, many warehouses are in cities like Lagos, Nairobi, or Johannesburg, where space is expensive. So you need to use every square meter wisely. For a small warehouse of 500 square meters, aim for 60% storage, 20% aisles, 10% receiving/shipping, and 10% packing and offices. Use a U-shaped flow: goods come in one side, get stored, picked, packed, and leave from the same side. This reduces travel distance. Keep fast-moving items near the packing area. For example, if you sell mobile phone accessories, put the most popular chargers within 10 meters of the packing table. Use wide aislesâat least 3 meters for forklifts, 1.5 meters for hand trucks. Label every location with a code like A-01-02 (Aisle A, Rack 1, Shelf 2). In hot climates, ensure ventilation and shade for temperature-sensitive goods like pharmaceuticals. Consider local materials: use locally made shelving from welders in Kano or Nairobi to cut costs. Draw your layout on paper first, then mark the floor with paint. Test with a stopwatch: how long does it take to pick 10 orders? Adjust until you minimize walking. Remember, a good layout can cut picking time by 30%.

lessons.title: Storage Systems and Material Handling Equipment
lessons.body: Choosing the right storage and handling equipment depends on your goods and budget. For small items like phone cases or cosmetics, use shelving units. A basic steel shelving unit (2m high, 1m wide, 0.5m deep) costs about $50 in Nairobi or Accra. For heavier items like bags of rice or cement, use pallet racks. A pallet rack with 3 levels can hold 1,000 kg per level and costs around $200 per bay. In many African warehouses, you'll see hand trucks (trolleys) for moving boxesâthey cost $30-$50. For heavier loads, use a manual pallet jack ($200-$300) or a forklift ($10,000 used). If you can't afford a forklift, use a pallet jack and ramps. For small operations, use plastic bins and labels. Stack boxes no more than 5 high to avoid crushing. Use the FIFO method: First In, First Out. Put older stock in front. For cold storage, like for vaccines or fresh produce, you need a refrigerated room (costs $5,000+). In rural areas, solar-powered cold rooms are becoming popular. Always train staff on safe lifting: bend knees, keep back straight, don't twist. A simple rule: if it's over 25 kg, use a trolley. Also, keep aisles clear. In dusty areas, cover goods with tarps. Regularly inspect equipmentâa broken pallet jack can injure someone. Invest in good locks and cages for high-value items like electronics.

lessons.title: Receiving, Put-away, and Picking Processes
lessons.body: Receiving starts when a truck arrives. First, check the delivery note against your purchase order. Count the boxes. If you ordered 100 cartons of cooking oil and only 98 arrive, note it on the delivery note and take a photo. Inspect for damage: dented boxes, leaks, or broken seals. In Africa, heat and rough roads cause damage, so be thorough. Sign only after counting. Then, put away items immediately. Use a location code system. For example, if you receive 50 cartons of soap, put them in location B-03-02. Record it in a notebook or a simple Excel sheet on your phone. For picking, you need a pick list. This is a list of items to collect for an order. Walk through the warehouse and pick items. Use a cart or trolley. Pick the oldest stock first (FIFO). For small items, use a bin system: each order gets a bin, and you scan or mark items. In busy warehouses, use a zone picking method: one person picks from aisles A-B, another from C-D. This speeds up the process. For example, a warehouse in Kampala handling 200 orders a day can cut picking time from 4 hours to 2.5 hours by zoning. Always double-check the picked items against the pick list before packing. Mistakes cost moneyâa wrong item shipped to a customer in another country means expensive returns. Use a simple barcode scanner ($50) or a smartphone app to verify. Keep the picking area clean and organized.

lessons.title: Packing, Shipping, and Returns Management
lessons.body: Packing protects goods and makes shipping easy. Use the right box size: too big and items shift; too small and they won't fit. For fragile items like glass or electronics, wrap in bubble wrap or newspaper. In Africa, many packers use locally available materials: banana leaves for padding, old cardboard boxes, and sisal twine. But for professional shipping, use corrugated boxes and packing tape. Label each box with the customer's name, address, and phone number. Include a packing slip inside. For shipping, choose a method: local courier (e.g., G4S, Sendy), bus companies (e.g., ABC Transport in Nigeria), or boda boda for last-mile. Always get a tracking number. For international shipping, use DHL or FedEx, but they are expensive. Consider consolidating shipments to save costs. For returns, have a clear policy: accept returns within 7 days if unused. Inspect returned items. If resalable, put back in stock. If damaged, repair or discard. Track return reasons: wrong size, damaged, late delivery. Use this data to improve. For example, if many returns are due to late delivery, change your courier. Keep a returns log with date, order number, reason, and action. In many African markets, customers expect easy returns, so a good returns process builds trust. Also, train staff to handle returns politely. A happy customer returns to buy again.

lessons.title: Inventory Management Techniques
lessons.body: Inventory is money sitting on shelves. Too much and you tie up cash; too little and you lose sales. Start by counting everything. Do a physical count every month. Use a simple system: a notebook or a free app like Zoho Inventory or Excel. For each item, record: item name, quantity, location, and reorder level. The reorder level is the minimum stock before you order more. For example, if you sell 10 bags of cement per day and it takes 3 days to restock, set reorder level at 40 bags (10 x 3 + 10 safety stock). Use ABC analysis: A items are high value (e.g., laptops), count weekly. B items are medium (e.g., phone chargers), count monthly. C items are low value (e.g., screws), count quarterly. This saves time. Use FIFO to avoid expiry. For perishables like food, use FEFO (First Expired, First Out). In Africa, power cuts can affect electronic records, so keep a paper backup. Train one person to be inventory manager. Do spot checks: pick 10 random items and verify counts. If discrepancies, investigate. Use cycle counting: count a small section daily instead of full counts. This keeps records accurate. Also, watch for theft. Keep high-value items in a locked cage. Use security cameras if possible. A good inventory system reduces stockouts by 50% and excess stock by 30%.

lessons.title: Warehouse Safety and Security
lessons.body: Safety first: warehouses have hazards like falling boxes, forklifts, and heavy lifting. Train all staff on safety rules. Wear closed shoes, gloves, and high-vis vests. Keep aisles clear. Stack boxes straight and not too high. Use ladders, not chairs, to reach high shelves. For forklifts, only trained operators should drive. Set a speed limit of 5 km/h. Put up mirrors at blind corners. In hot climates, provide water and shade to prevent heat exhaustion. Have a first aid kit and fire extinguisher. Check them monthly. For security, control who enters. Use a logbook for visitors. Install locks on doors and windows. For high-value goods, use a cage or safe. Consider hiring a night guard. In many African cities, security is a major concern. Use CCTV cameras ($100 each) if affordable. Keep the perimeter well-lit. Do not leave cash in the warehouse. Do bank deposits daily. For fire safety, no smoking. Store flammable liquids separately. Have an evacuation plan and practice it every 6 months. Also, secure the loading dock: only authorized trucks. Check driver IDs. For cyber security, if you use inventory software, use strong passwords and backup data. Insurance: get warehouse insurance to cover fire, theft, and flood. A basic policy costs about 0.5% of stock value per year. Report all incidents, even minor cuts. A safe warehouse is a productive warehouse.

quiz.q: What is the recommended percentage of storage space in a small warehouse layout?
quiz.explanation: A good layout uses about 60% for storage, 20% aisles, 10% receiving/shipping, and 10% packing/offices.

quiz.q: Which flow pattern reduces travel distance in a warehouse?
quiz.explanation: U-shaped flow allows goods to enter and leave from the same side, minimizing travel.

quiz.q: What is the minimum aisle width for a forklift?
quiz.explanation: Forklifts need at least 3 meters for safe operation.

quiz.q: Which item should be stored closest to the packing area?
quiz.explanation: Fast-moving items should be near packing to reduce picking time.

quiz.q: What does the location code A-01-02 represent?
quiz.explanation: The code typically means Aisle A, Rack 1, Shelf 2.

quiz.q: What is a cost-effective storage option for small items?
quiz.explanation: Shelving units are inexpensive and suitable for small items.

quiz.q: What is the maximum recommended stacking height for boxes to avoid crushing?
quiz.explanation: Stacking more than 5 high can crush lower boxes.

quiz.q: What does FIFO stand for?
quiz.explanation: FIFO means First In, First Out, ensuring older stock is used first.

quiz.q: Which equipment is best for moving heavy pallets without a forklift?
quiz.explanation: A pallet jack can move heavy pallets manually.

quiz.q: What should you do if a delivery arrives with damaged boxes?
options: C) Note on delivery note and take photo
quiz.explanation: Document damage on the delivery note and take photos for claims.

quiz.q: What is a pick list?
options: A) List of items to order
B) List of items to collect for an order
quiz.explanation: A pick list tells pickers which items and quantities to collect.

quiz.q: What is zone picking?
options: A) Picking all items from one zone
B) Assigning pickers to specific zones
quiz.explanation: Zone picking assigns each picker to a specific area to speed up the process.

quiz.q: Why is double-checking picked items important?
options: B) To reduce errors and returns
quiz.explanation: Double-checking prevents wrong items from being shipped, saving money on returns.

quiz.q: What is a good packing material for fragile items?
quiz.explanation: Bubble wrap provides cushioning for fragile items.

quiz.q: What should be included inside a shipped box?
quiz.explanation: A packing slip lists the contents for the customer and for tracking.

quiz.q: What is a common last-mile delivery method in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Boda boda (motorcycle taxis) are widely used for last-mile delivery in African cities.

quiz.q: What is the typical return window for many African retailers?
quiz.explanation: A 7-day return window is common and builds customer trust.

quiz.q: What should you do with a returned item that is resalable?
quiz.explanation: Resalable returns should be put back into inventory.

quiz.q: What is the reorder level for an item selling 10 units per day with a 3-day lead time and 10 units safety stock?
quiz.explanation: Reorder level = (10 x 3) + 10 = 40 units.

quiz.q: What does ABC analysis classify?
quiz.explanation: ABC analysis groups items by value: A high, B medium, C low.

quiz.q: How often should A items be counted?
quiz.explanation: A items are high value, so they should be counted weekly.

quiz.q: What is FEFO?
quiz.explanation: FEFO ensures items with the earliest expiry are shipped first.

quiz.q: Why keep a paper backup of inventory records?
options: B) In case of power cuts
quiz.explanation: Power cuts are common in Africa, so paper backups prevent data loss.

quiz.q: What is cycle counting?
options: A) Counting all inventory at once
B) Counting a small section daily
quiz.explanation: Cycle counting involves counting small sections regularly to maintain accuracy.

quiz.q: What is a key safety rule for lifting heavy boxes?
options: B) Bend knees, keep back straight
quiz.explanation: Bending knees and keeping the back straight prevents injury.

quiz.q: What should be provided to prevent heat exhaustion in hot warehouses?
quiz.explanation: Water and shade help prevent heat-related illnesses.

quiz.q: How often should fire extinguishers be checked?
quiz.explanation: Monthly checks ensure extinguishers are ready for use.

quiz.q: What is a security measure for high-value goods?
quiz.explanation: A locked cage restricts access to high-value items.

quiz.q: What should be done with cash in the warehouse?
quiz.explanation: Daily bank deposits reduce theft risk.

quiz.q: What is the approximate annual cost of warehouse insurance?
quiz.explanation: Basic warehouse insurance typically costs about 0.5% of stock value per year.
